subtopic_detail: A student referred with presumed depression whose knees buckle when he laughs and whose mood is fully reactive
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 22 year old engineering student referred by his general practitioner with a working diagnosis of depression. For eighteen months he has felt overwhelmingly sleepy during the day, falls asleep in lectures despite trying to stay awake, and has failed two subjects.

He describes his naps as short and refreshing, and he wakes from them feeling clear for an hour or two. When you ask what happens when something strikes him as very funny, he says that laughing hard with his housemates makes his knees give way and his jaw go slack for about half a minute while he stays fully aware of what people are saying. On some mornings he wakes unable to move for a minute or so and has seen a figure standing in the doorway as he falls asleep. He goes to bed at eleven, sleeps eight hours undisturbed, does not snore, and his body mass index is 22 kg/m2. He still plays in his band and enjoys it, and his mood lifts when he is with friends.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect with normal range, no psychomotor retardation, normal cranial nerve and peripheral neurological examination, no goitre, body mass index 22 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 5 out of 27, full blood count, iron studies with ferritin 84 mcg/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone and liver function tests within normal limits, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Sleep history: Bedtime 11 pm with eight hours of undisturbed sleep, no snoring or witnessed apnoeas, refreshing daytime naps of 15 to 20 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his assessment?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review his mood again in four weeks
options.rationale: His mood is reactive, he retains enjoyment of his band and his depression score is low, so the referral diagnosis is not supported, and starting an antidepressant would obscure the picture. Antidepressants do have a role later for the muscle weakness episodes, but only after the diagnosis is established (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

options.text: Start modafinil 200 mg each morning and review his sleepiness in a month
options.rationale: Modafinil is a mainstay of treatment but Australian access through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme requires a confirmed diagnosis with objective sleep study evidence, and empirical treatment would remove the ability to obtain that evidence. Stimulant treatment before diagnosis also risks masking another sleep disorder (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

options.text: Arrange overnight home oximetry to assess for obstructive sleep apnoea
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea is argued against by the absence of snoring or witnessed apnoeas, a body mass index of 22 kg/m2, undisturbed nocturnal sleep and naps that are refreshing rather than unrefreshing. Oximetry would also miss the daytime findings that carry the diagnosis (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

options.text: Advise a regular sleep schedule and review him again in three months
options.rationale: Insufficient sleep syndrome and delayed sleep phase are the common causes of student sleepiness, but he already sleeps eight hours on a regular schedule and neither explains episodes of sudden bilateral muscle weakness with preserved awareness. Three months of watchful waiting also risks another failed semester (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with retained awareness, together with sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and refreshing naps, is the classic tetrad, and confirmation requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes followed the next day by a multiple sleep latency test. The diagnostic thresholds are a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy).

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 arises from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons and has a mean diagnostic delay of around ten years, most often misattributed to depression, laziness or insufficient sleep. Cataplexy is the specific feature and is frequently missed because patients describe it as feeling weak or wobbly when laughing rather than as a neurological event, and consciousness is always preserved, which separates it from seizures and syncope. Diagnosis rests on overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes of sleepiness followed by a multiple sleep latency test showing a mean latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods, and cerebrospinal fluid orexin below 110 pg/mL is an alternative confirmatory test. Treatment separates the sleepiness, managed with modafinil, dexamfetamine or sodium oxybate, from cataplexy, managed with venlafaxine or a tricyclic. Australian driving fitness standards require the condition to be reported and adequately controlled before commercial driving is permitted.
key_points: Cataplexy is sudden bilateral muscle weakness triggered by emotion with preserved awareness
Refreshing short naps distinguish narcolepsy from the unrefreshing sleep of apnoea and depression
Diagnosis requires polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
A mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two sleep onset rapid eye movement periods is diagnostic
Sleepiness and cataplexy are treated with different drug classes
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically what happens when the patient laughs hard, hears a joke or is caught by surprise, because patients almost never volunteer cataplexy and will describe it as clumsiness or weak knees rather than as anything neurological.

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of shoulder and hip girdle pain with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 68 and no cranial symptoms
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in clinic seeing a 71 year old woman with six weeks of pain across both shoulders and both hips that came on over about a week. She cannot lift her arms to wash her hair or get out of a low chair without pushing off with her hands, and her husband has been helping her dress in the mornings.

She describes stiffness lasting about ninety minutes after waking that eases through the day, and she wakes at night when she rolls onto a shoulder. She has lost 2 kg and feels generally tired. She has had no headache, no scalp tenderness, no pain in her jaw on chewing and no visual disturbance, and her temporal arteries are non tender with normal pulsation. On examination shoulder and hip movement is limited by pain rather than by weakness, and power is 5 out of 5 when tested against resistance in short arcs. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 68 mm/h with a C reactive protein of 42 mg/L, and her creatine kinase is 92 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, blood pressure 142/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Painful restriction of active shoulder abduction and hip flexion with full passive range, power 5 out of 5 in short arcs, no synovitis of hands or wrists, non tender temporal arteries with normal pulsation
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h (less than 30), C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), creatine kinase 92 U/L (30-180), rheumatoid factor and cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start prednisolone 50 mg orally daily and arrange a temporal artery biopsy
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid with urgent biopsy is the response to cranial arteritis, which requires headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms, none of which is present here. Using that dose for girdle symptoms alone exposes her to unnecessary steroid toxicity (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica).

options.text: Start prednisolone 15 mg orally daily and review her within one week
options.rationale: Girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness in a woman over 50 with raised inflammatory markers, a normal creatine kinase and pain limited movement rather than true weakness fits the clinical diagnosis, and the standard starting dose is 12.5 to 25 mg daily. Early review matters because a dramatic response within a few days is part of the diagnosis and its absence should prompt reconsideration (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica).

options.text: Start methotrexate 10 mg orally weekly with folic acid supplementation
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a steroid sparing agent added for relapsing disease or where steroid toxicity is a particular concern, and it takes six to twelve weeks to act. Starting it alone leaves her untreated through the period when her symptoms are worst (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Start naproxen 500 mg orally twice daily and review her in four weeks
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs produce only partial relief in this condition, and a poor response to them is one of the classification criteria rather than a reason to persist. Four weeks of an incomplete trial in a woman of 71 also carries gastrointestinal and renal risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Arrange MRI of both shoulders before starting any specific treatment
options.rationale: Imaging may show subacromial bursitis and biceps tenosynovitis but these findings are supportive rather than diagnostic, and the diagnosis is clinical with a therapeutic response as confirmation. Bilateral simultaneous girdle involvement also argues against the rotator cuff pathology that shoulder MRI would be looking for (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica).

explanation.summary: Polymyalgia rheumatica affects people over 50, most commonly in their seventies, and presents with bilateral shoulder and often pelvic girdle pain, morning stiffness beyond 45 minutes, and raised inflammatory markers. The critical bedside distinction is that the limitation is due to pain rather than weakness, with a normal creatine kinase, which separates it from inflammatory myositis. Around 15 to 20 per cent of patients have or develop giant cell arteritis, so every review asks about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms, since visual loss is irreversible and needs immediate high dose steroid. Treatment starts at 12.5 to 25 mg of prednisolone daily with a response expected within days, followed by a slow taper over one to two years, and relapse during tapering is common. Bone protection with calcium, vitamin D and a bisphosphonate is considered from the outset given the duration of steroid exposure.
key_points: Girdle pain limited by pain rather than weakness with a normal creatine kinase
Starting prednisolone dose is 12.5 to 25 mg daily, not the higher arteritis dose
A dramatic response within days supports the diagnosis and its absence should prompt review
Screen for cranial arteritis symptoms at diagnosis and at every subsequent visit
Plan bone protection because treatment typically runs one to two years
explanation.pearls: If girdle symptoms have not substantially improved within a week of starting 15 mg of prednisolone daily, reconsider the diagnosis rather than increasing the dose, because late onset seronegative rheumatoid arthritis and occult malignancy both present this way and respond only partially.

subtopic_detail: A groin lump that comes and goes with crying in a six week old born at 32 weeks, alongside an incidental umbilical swelling
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a six week old boy brought by his parents who have noticed a lump in his right groin. It appears when he cries or strains and disappears when he settles, and they first saw it four days ago.

He was born at 32 weeks gestation and spent three weeks in the special care nursery before going home, and he is now feeding well and gaining 32 g a day. He has had no vomiting, his nappies are normal and he has been settled between feeds. On examination there is a soft swelling above and lateral to the right pubic tubercle that you can reduce easily with gentle pressure, and it is not tender, discoloured or fixed. Both testes are in the scrotum. His abdomen is soft and not distended. You also note a 15 mm umbilical swelling that reduces easily with a defect you can feel around its edge.

data_table.Examination: Soft easily reducible right groin swelling above and lateral to the pubic tubercle, non tender with normal overlying skin, both testes descended, soft non distended abdomen, 15 mm easily reducible umbilical swelling with a palpable fascial edge
data_table.Growth: Weight gain 32 g per day, tracking along the 25th centile corrected for gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the groin swelling?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review both swellings again when he is twelve months old
options.rationale: Spontaneous closure is the expected course for the umbilical swelling, which is why that one is observed to school age, but the groin swelling arises through a patent processus vaginalis that does not close and can trap bowel. Applying the umbilical rule to the groin is the error this pairing is built around (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the groin before deciding whether he needs referral
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical when a reducible swelling appears with straining above and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and imaging is reserved for an equivocal examination or for distinguishing a hydrocele of the cord. Waiting for a scan adds days of incarceration risk without changing the plan (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Refer him to a paediatric surgeon for repair within the next few days
options.rationale: Incarceration risk is highest in the first months of life and higher again in infants born preterm, running at roughly 30 per cent in the first year for this age group, so repair is arranged promptly rather than electively. Reducibility today does not lower that risk, since incarceration is an unpredictable event rather than the endpoint of a gradual process (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Refer him for elective repair on a routine list after his first birthday
options.rationale: Routine listing is appropriate for an older child in whom incarceration risk has fallen substantially, but a six week old born at 32 weeks sits in the highest risk group. An incarcerated hernia in this age group threatens both the bowel and the testis (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

options.text: Apply a supportive binder over the groin and review him again in six weeks
options.rationale: Trusses and binders have no role in children, do not prevent incarceration and can cause skin breakdown and pressure injury to the cord structures. They also give false reassurance to parents who then delay presenting when the swelling becomes irreducible (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia).

explanation.summary: Inguinal hernia in infancy is almost always indirect and results from failure of the processus vaginalis to obliterate, so it never resolves spontaneously and always requires operative repair. Incidence is around 1 to 5 per cent of term infants and rises to 10 to 30 per cent in those born preterm, with boys affected far more often than girls. The urgency comes from incarceration, which is commonest under one year of age and carries risks of bowel ischaemia, testicular infarction from compression of the cord vessels and, in girls, strangulation of an ovary within the sac. An incarcerated hernia that cannot be reduced needs immediate surgical attention, while one reduced successfully is usually repaired on that admission after a period of settling. The umbilical hernia is managed entirely differently, closing spontaneously in the great majority and only being repaired if it persists beyond about four to five years or complicates, which is very rare.
key_points: Infant inguinal hernia never closes spontaneously and always needs repair
Incarceration risk is highest under one year and higher again after preterm birth
The diagnosis is clinical and does not require imaging when the examination is typical
Umbilical hernias close spontaneously and are observed until about four to five years
Trusses and binders have no place in paediatric hernia management
explanation.pearls: A groin swelling above and lateral to the pubic tubercle that extends towards the scrotum is a hernia, whereas one that is confined to the scrotum, transilluminates and does not extend up the cord is a hydrocele, and only the first needs a surgical appointment within days.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Paediatric surgery referral guidelines

subtopic_detail: Two years of cramping pain confined to the first two days of each period in a sixteen year old missing school
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16 year old girl who has come with her mother about painful periods. Her periods started at twelve and became regular at fourteen, arriving every 28 to 30 days and lasting five days.

For the past two years she has had cramping lower abdominal pain that begins a few hours before the bleeding starts, is worst on the first day, and has settled by the end of the second day. It is associated with nausea and loose stools on the first day, and she has missed one or two days of school in most months this year. She has no pain at any other time in the cycle, no pain with bowel movements or urination outside her period, and she is not sexually active. Abdominal examination is normal with no masses and no tenderness today, and she is on day nineteen of her cycle. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g when the pain starts with little effect.

data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen with no palpable mass, normal external genitalia, no pelvic examination performed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and ferritin within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start regular ibuprofen beginning as the pain starts each cycle
options.rationale: Prostaglandin driven myometrial contraction produces this pattern, and a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug taken regularly rather than as needed inhibits its synthesis and relieves pain in about 70 to 80 per cent of adolescents. Her failure on paracetamol does not predict failure on this class because the mechanisms differ (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound before starting any medical treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the history suggests a secondary cause, such as pain outside menstruation, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, or failure of first line treatment, and none of those applies to pain confined to the first two days. A transabdominal scan also has limited sensitivity for the conditions being sought (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without a break
options.rationale: Hormonal suppression is an effective second line option and a reasonable first choice when contraception is also wanted, but it is not the standard first step for uncomplicated pain of this pattern. Continuous use without a hormone free interval belongs to management of suspected endometriosis rather than to initial treatment (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Refer her for diagnostic laparoscopy to look for endometriosis now
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is considered after failure of both a non steroidal agent and hormonal treatment, or where symptoms point to a secondary cause, because a general anaesthetic and a negative finding are otherwise likely. Pain strictly confined to the first two days without acyclical symptoms is the pattern least associated with endometriosis (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea).

options.text: Prescribe codeine with paracetamol to be taken on the worst days
options.rationale: Opioids are not recommended for menstrual pain in adolescents because they do not address prostaglandin mediated contraction, worsen the nausea and constipation already present, and carry dependence risk. Codeine is also contraindicated under 18 years in several settings owing to variable metabolism (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhoea typically begins six to twenty four months after menarche once ovulatory cycles establish, and is characterised by cramping suprapubic pain starting just before or with the bleeding and lasting one to three days, often with nausea, diarrhoea and headache from systemic prostaglandin effects. Secondary causes are suggested by pain outside menstruation, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, heavy or irregular bleeding, onset at menarche without a pain free interval, or failure of first line treatment, and these prompt imaging and specialist referral. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line and work best when started at the first sign of pain and continued regularly through the worst forty eight hours rather than taken reactively. Hormonal treatment with a combined pill, progestogen or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device is second line or first line where contraception is also required. Repeated school absence is itself an indication to treat actively rather than to reassure.
key_points: Primary dysmenorrhoea begins six to twenty four months after menarche with ovulatory cycles
Pain confined to the first one to three days of bleeding is the characteristic pattern
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs taken regularly are first line
Acyclical pain, dyspareunia or treatment failure prompt imaging and referral
Opioids have no place in routine management of menstrual pain in adolescents
explanation.pearls: Advise starting the non steroidal agent at the first twinge or the day before bleeding is expected and continuing it regularly for 48 to 72 hours, because these drugs prevent prostaglandin synthesis rather than reversing its effects and taking them once the pain is established is why most adolescents report they do not work.

subtopic_detail: Seven months of early morning waking in a woman whose sleep diary shows nine and a half hours in bed for five and a half hours of sleep
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 47 year old accountant who has had seven months of broken sleep. She falls asleep easily but wakes at about three each morning and lies awake for an hour and a half or more, watching the clock and working out how little sleep she will get.

She now goes to bed at nine thirty to give herself the best chance and stays in bed until seven, and her two week sleep diary shows an average of nine and a half hours in bed for five and a half hours of sleep. She is tired and irritable during the day but does not doze off, and she has not fallen asleep while driving. She denies low mood and still enjoys her weekly choir, scoring 4 on the Patient Health Questionnaire 9. Her husband reports no snoring, gasping or leg kicking. She drinks two standard drinks a week, works regular office hours, and a two week course of temazepam three months ago helped while she took it. She is asking for a further prescription.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, Mallampati class 2, no goitre, normal cardiorespiratory and neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 4 out of 27, full blood count, ferritin 96 mcg/L (30-200), thyroid stimulating hormone and iron studies within normal limits
data_table.Sleep diary: Average time in bed nine and a half hours, average total sleep time five and a half hours, sleep onset within fifteen minutes, one prolonged awakening from around 3 am

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg nightly and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine hypnotics are recommended only for short term intermittent use of up to two to four weeks because tolerance, rebound insomnia and dependence develop with nightly use, and three months of unmonitored supply invites all three. The fact that it worked previously reflects its short term efficacy rather than its suitability for a chronic problem (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence).

options.text: Start quetiapine 25 mg nightly for its sedating effect on sleep onset
options.rationale: Low dose quetiapine is widely prescribed off label for sleep but has no efficacy evidence for insomnia disorder and carries metabolic, extrapyramidal and cardiac risk. Her difficulty is maintaining sleep rather than initiating it, so a sedating agent addresses the wrong part of the night (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start mirtazapine 15 mg nightly and review her sleep in four weeks time
options.rationale: A sedating antidepressant is a reasonable choice when insomnia accompanies a depressive disorder, but her score of 4 with preserved enjoyment does not support that diagnosis. Treating primary insomnia with an antidepressant also brings weight gain and daytime sedation without addressing the behavioural maintenance of the problem (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer her for a structured cognitive behavioural therapy programme for insomnia
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder in Australian and international guidance, with effects that outlast hypnotics, and its sleep restriction component directly targets the nine and a half hours in bed that are diluting her sleep. Her prolonged time in bed and clock watching are the maintaining behaviours the programme is designed to reverse (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Insomnia).

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene measures alone and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene education as a stand alone treatment performs barely better than control in trials and is the weakest component of the multi part therapy, because it does not change the time in bed or the conditioned arousal that maintain chronic insomnia. It is included within the structured programme rather than used instead of it (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Insomnia).

explanation.summary: Insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least three nights a week for at least three months with daytime consequences, despite adequate opportunity for sleep. The most common and most reversible maintaining factor is extending time in bed to compensate, which lowers sleep efficiency and strengthens the association between bed and being awake. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia combines sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relaxation and sleep hygiene, and it is first line because its benefits persist after treatment ends whereas hypnotic benefits do not. Before diagnosing primary insomnia, screen for obstructive sleep apnoea, restless legs syndrome, depression, alcohol use, shift work and medications such as stimulants and corticosteroids. Where medication is needed as a bridge, the recommendation is the lowest effective dose intermittently for no more than two to four weeks with an agreed exit plan.
key_points: Insomnia disorder needs symptoms three nights a week for three months with daytime impact
Excessive time in bed lowers sleep efficiency and maintains the problem
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and outlasts hypnotics
Sleep hygiene alone is the weakest single component and is not adequate treatment
Hypnotics are for short term intermittent use with a planned exit
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction sets time in bed to roughly the average total sleep time from the diary, with a floor of five hours, and expands it by fifteen minutes each week once sleep efficiency exceeds 85 per cent, which is why the therapy briefly makes people sleepier before it makes them better.
